intro.name: The beginning
intro.text: Woven mats line the clearing. Potters display bowls and jars; weavers offer baskets and patterned cloth; woodcarvers show paddles, ornaments, and masks; craftspeople bring shell jewelry, musical instruments, toys, and ingenious household tools. Visitors barter food, materials, and favors. A loud, merciless judge has been invited to award the festival's highest honor.

choices.label: MAKE THE FAIR A CEREMONIAL FESTIVAL.

variants.text:
Woven mats line the clearing. Potters display bowls and jars; weavers offer baskets and patterned cloth; woodcarvers show paddles, ornaments, and masks; craftspeople bring shell jewelry, musical instruments, toys, and ingenious household tools. Visitors barter food, materials, and favors. A loud, merciless judge has been invited to award the festival's highest honor.
The fair celebrates the village's first thriving settlement. The Golden Child may make an astonishing miniature sculpture or solve a kiln-design problem, then wander off to play with the other children.

Woven mats line the clearing. Potters display bowls and jars; weavers offer baskets and patterned cloth; woodcarvers show paddles, ornaments, and masks; craftspeople bring shell jewelry, musical instruments, toys, and ingenious household tools. Visitors barter food, materials, and favors. A loud, merciless judge has been invited to award the festival's highest honor.
The Lost Children contribute tiny clay animals and painted shells. A competition may honor the founders, the totems, or the Great Falls; an elder discovers a child's apparently childish design is more practical than a master's.

Woven mats line the clearing. Potters display bowls and jars; weavers offer baskets and patterned cloth; woodcarvers show paddles, ornaments, and masks; craftspeople bring shell jewelry, musical instruments, toys, and ingenious household tools. Visitors barter food, materials, and favors. A loud, merciless judge has been invited to award the festival's highest honor.
The Tribal Chief opens the fair and arbitrates disputes.

Woven mats line the clearing. Potters display bowls and jars; weavers offer baskets and patterned cloth; woodcarvers show paddles, ornaments, and masks; craftspeople bring shell jewelry, musical instruments, toys, and ingenious household tools. Visitors barter food, materials, and favors. A loud, merciless judge has been invited to award the festival's highest honor.
Sculptors and potters incorporate fallen leaves and non-damaging natural motifs. A dispute arises when someone wants to remove living material from the Tree; the villagers must choose preservation or artistic ambition.

Woven mats line the clearing. Potters display bowls and jars; weavers offer baskets and patterned cloth; woodcarvers show paddles, ornaments, and masks; craftspeople bring shell jewelry, musical instruments, toys, and ingenious household tools. Visitors barter food, materials, and favors. A loud, merciless judge has been invited to award the festival's highest honor.
Villagers and Heathens/Isolans can enter as makers, judges, critics, traders, and spectators. Rival groups accuse each other of stealing designs; an Isolan judge may fairly award a prize to a villager, or a village judge may publicly praise an Isolan rival. A mixed team may win the highest honor, provoking either reconciliation or a boycott.

text_only.reason: narrative: visitors barter; no food changes hands in the village stores

a1.text: The Judge Who Feared No Craft: The judge calls a bowl 'a coconut shell pretending to be important' and a basket 'a nest with delusions.' Then (judge.he/she) praises a shy child's tiny woven fish as the best work at the fair. The crowd erupts in applause.

a2.text: The Great Upset: A novice defeats a celebrated master. The master demands a recount; the judges confirm the result.

text_only.reason: narrative: 'celebrated' is part of the story, not a change the event makes

a3.text: The Perfectly Useless Wonder: A contraption is exquisite, intricate, and entirely incapable of doing what its maker claims. The judges award it a special prize for imagination.

a4.text: The Rigged Prize: A judge secretly favors a relative. A witness exposes the bias; the council orders a new judging panel.

a5.text: The Shared Victory: Two rivals create an extraordinary object together and refuse to claim individual credit. Both receive recognition.

b1.text: A Village of Artisans: Techniques spread across households.

text_only.reason: rule 8: no game has a Crafting skill

b2.text: The Great Barter Disaster: One villager trades an entire basket of food for a 'rare sacred pebble' that turns out to be ordinary stone.

text_only.reason: narrative: one villager's basket of food, not the village stores

b3.text: The Invention Exchange: A potter and weaver combine techniques to create an unexpectedly useful container.

b4.text: The Lost Heirloom: A treasured family ornament vanishes amid the crowd. The search ends in recovery, an accusation, or an awkward discovery that its owner put it in the wrong basket.

text_only.reason: narrative: an ornament goes missing, not a villager

b5.text: The Children's Fair: Children begin trading miniature clay animals, shell necklaces, and painted stones. The adults realize their fair has been thoroughly outshone.

c1.text: The Night of a Hundred Lamps: Safe, sheltered firelight illuminates the exhibits as singers recite the makers' names. The festival becomes an annual tradition.

c2.text: The Uninvited Storm: Rain sweeps through the clearing. Potters rush to protect unfired work, while the weavers rescue their dyes and fibers. A hastily built shelter inspires a new communal structure.

c3.text: The Mask That Chose Its Owner: A ceremonial mask repeatedly falls toward the same villager. Some see a sign; others find a crooked stand.

c4.text: The Feast of Reconciliation: Two feuding households exchange handmade gifts and begin speaking again.

c5.text: The Fair Nobody Could End: The celebrations run so long that farming and building are neglected. The elders establish sensible festival hours next time.
